Javascript Introduction

JavaScript is the programming language of the web. It can update and change both HTML and CSS. It can calculate, manipulate and validate data.

  • While HTML structures the content and CSS styles it, JavaScript controls the behavior. It runs directly in the browser and can react to user actions, update content without reloading the page, and connect with servers to fetch data (like in live search or chat apps).
  • JavaScript is not limited to just web pages. With modern tools and frameworks like Node.js, React, and Angular, it is used for building full web applications, mobile apps, games, and even server-side development. Its flexibility makes it one of the most popular programming languages in the world.

JavaScript Where To

JavaScript can be written directly inside an HTML file using the script tag. It is usually placed either in the head section or just before the closing body tag. You can also write JavaScript in a separate file with a .js extension and link it to your HTML file. This helps keep the code clean and easier to manage.

1. JavaScript is a popular programming language used to create dynamic and interactive websites.

2. It allows web pages to respond to user actions, such as clicking buttons, filling forms, or moving the mouse.

3. JavaScript works together with HTML and CSS to build complete and functional websites.

4. It can be written directly inside the HTML file or linked through external JavaScript files.

5. JavaScript runs in the browser, which means users don’t need to install anything extra to use it.

6. With JavaScript, developers can change the content of a webpage without reloading the entire page.

7. JavaScript is used in many web applications, including games, form validation, and interactive charts.

8. Modern frameworks like React, Angular, and Vue are built on JavaScript to create powerful applications.

9. JavaScript is also used on the server-side using platforms like Node.js, making it a full-stack language.

10. Learning JavaScript is essential for anyone interested in web development, as it brings websites to life.

JS Syntax

JavaScript syntax is the set of rules that define how the language should be written and understood. It includes the correct way to use variables, functions, loops, conditions, and other elements. Every JavaScript statement usually ends with a semicolon, though it’s optional in some cases. These statements are the basic building blocks of your code and are executed in the order they appear unless told otherwise by control structures.

Variables are used to store data values and can be declared using keywords like var, let, or const. Each of these has its own rules—‘let’ and ‘const’ are block-scoped and more modern, while ‘var’ is function-scoped and older. JavaScript is case-sensitive, meaning `myVariable` and `myvariable` would be treated as different names. Strings must be enclosed in quotes, numbers don’t need them, and comments can be added using double slashes (//) or a slash-asterisk block (/* */).

Functions in JavaScript are reusable blocks of code designed to perform a task. They are declared using the function keyword, followed by a name, parentheses, and curly braces. Inside the braces, you write the code that will run when the function is called. JavaScript also uses curly braces to group blocks of code for conditions (like if-else) and loops (like for or while), making it clear where logic starts and ends. Understanding syntax is the first step to writing error-free, well-structured code in JavaScript.

    Always use clear and meaningful variable names. Instead of using short names like x or a, use names like userName or totalPrice. This makes your code easier to understand and maintain, especially when projects grow larger.

    Consistently use indentation and spacing. Proper formatting does not affect how the code runs but makes it much easier to read and debug. Following good formatting habits helps you and others quickly spot errors or understand logic flow.

In this guide, we learn the basics of HTML, which includes HTML tags ( <h1>, <p>, <img>, etc), attributes, elements, and document structure which collectively form a working web page.

JavaScript Comments

JavaScript comments are used to explain code, make it more readable, and help with debugging by temporarily disabling parts of code during development.

There are two main types of comments in JavaScript:

  1. Single-line Comments – These start with // and are used for short explanations or notes on the same line as code.
    Example:
    // This is a single-line comment
  2. Multi-line Comments – These start with /* and end with */. They are useful for adding detailed descriptions or commenting out blocks of code.
    Example:
    /* This is a multi-line comment
    It spans multiple lines */

JavaScript Comments

JavaScript comments are pieces of code that the JavaScript engine ignores during execution. They are used to explain code, make it more readable, and help developers debug or disable code temporarily. Comments are essential for collaboration and maintenance, especially in large projects.

Table of Contents

  • 1. Why Use Comments in JavaScript?
  • 2. Types of Comments
  • 3. Examples
  • 4. Tips & Best Practices
  • 5. When Not to Use Comments

1. Why Use Comments in JavaScript?

Comments in JavaScript help developers:

  • Understand the purpose of the code
  • Improve collaboration with other developers
  • Temporarily disable a block of code during debugging
  • Leave reminders or TODO notes

2. Types of Comments

  1. Single-line Comment (//):
    Used for brief explanations.
    // This is a single-line comment
  2. Multi-line Comment (/* ... */):
    Useful for longer descriptions or disabling code blocks.
    /* This is a multi-line comment
    It can span multiple lines */

3. Examples


        // Declare a variable
        let name = "John"; // user's name
        
        /* 
          This function greets the user
          using an alert dialog box 
        */
        function greet() {
          alert("Hello, " + name + "!");
        }

4. Tips & Best Practices

  • Write clear and concise comments that explain *why*, not just *what* the code does.
  • Keep comments up-to-date as code changes.
  • Use comments to mark TODOs and FIXMEs for future improvements.
  • Use comments to separate sections of code for better readability.

5. When Not to Use Comments

  • Don’t state the obvious — avoid comments that restate the code (e.g., // add 1 to i for i++).
  • Avoid clutter — too many comments can be as confusing as no comments at all.
  • Don’t leave outdated or misleading comments in the codebase.

Conclusion

JavaScript comments are powerful tools for improving the clarity and maintainability of your code. Use them wisely to document your thought process, debug efficiently, and collaborate effectively. Well-commented code is a hallmark of a professional developer.

JavaScript Variables

JavaScript Variables are containers for storing data values. Variables allow you to store and manipulate data in your scripts. They are fundamental building blocks in JavaScript programming.

You can declare a variable using var, let, or const keywords depending on the use case. let and const are modern and preferred over var in most scenarios.

Syntax

let variableName = value;

JavaScript Variable Code Example:

In this example, a variable called name is declared using let and stores a string value.

blocks.code: JavaScript Variable Demo

blocks.value:
Some Key Points About JavaScript Variables

1. Syntax:

  • Variables in JavaScript can be declared using var, let, or const.
  • The general syntax is: let variableName = value;
  • Example: let age = 25;

2. Case Sensitivity:

  • JavaScript is case-sensitive. age and Age are treated as different variables.
  • Always use consistent casing (e.g., camelCase) for readability.

Understanding Variable Scope

Variables declared with var have function scope, while let and const have block scope. This affects where they can be accessed in your code.

Example: In the example below, the variable message is declared using let, and can only be accessed inside the block it was declared in.


        {
          let message = "Hello, world!";
          console.log(message); // Works fine
        }
        console.log(message); // Error: message is not defined

Important Points About JavaScript Variables

1. Use `let`, `const`, or `var` to Declare Variables:

In JavaScript, you can declare variables using let, const, or var. It's recommended to use let for variables that will change and const for values that should remain constant. Avoid using var in modern JavaScript unless necessary, as it can lead to unexpected behavior due to function scoping.

2. Variable Names are Case-Sensitive:

JavaScript is case-sensitive, so username and UserName are treated as two different variables. Use consistent naming conventions like camelCase to avoid confusion and improve code readability.

3. Don't Use Reserved Keywords:

You cannot use JavaScript reserved words like function, return, class, or new as variable names. Doing so will result in a syntax error. Always choose meaningful, descriptive names.

4. Variables Can Hold Any Data Type:

JavaScript variables are dynamically typed. This means a variable can hold a number, string, boolean, array, object, or even a function. For example:

Example:

        let name = "Ashrita";
        let age = 20;
        let isStudent = true;
        let skills = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];

Each of these variables holds a different data type, and JavaScript handles them dynamically during runtime.

Summing up!

Understanding how to properly declare and use variables is a fundamental step in learning JavaScript. Use modern keywords like let and const, choose clear names, and take advantage of JavaScript’s flexibility with data types to write efficient and readable code.

JavaScript const

The const keyword in JavaScript is used to declare variables whose values are not meant to be reassigned. Once a variable is declared with const, its identifier cannot be reassigned to a different value. However, if it refers to objects or arrays, the contents of those objects or arrays can still be modified.

Example: Here, we declare a constant using const and attempt to reassign it, which throws an error.

blocks.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
  <script>
    const name = "Ashrita";
    document.write("Name: " + name);

    // Uncommenting the line below will throw an error:
    // name = "Anu"; // ❌ TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
  </script>
</body>
</html>

blocks.value:
Code Overview:

In the example above, the variable name is declared using const and holds a string value. Trying to reassign a new value to name will throw a TypeError.

JavaScript const Characteristics

  • Block Scoped: const declarations are block-scoped, meaning they are only accessible within the block in which they are defined.
  • Must Be Initialized: You must assign an initial value to a const variable at the time of declaration.
  • Cannot Be Reassigned: Reassigning a const variable results in a TypeError.
  • Objects and Arrays: The contents of objects and arrays declared with const can be changed, but the reference cannot.

Object Example:

The below code shows how you can modify properties of a constant object:

blocks.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
  <script>
    const person = { name: "Ashrita", age: 20 };
    person.age = 21; // ✅ allowed
    document.write("Updated Age: " + person.age);

    // person = {}; ❌ Not allowed – reassignment throws an error
  </script>
</body>
</html>

blocks.value:
Array Example:

The example below shows that const arrays can have their elements changed or added, but the array itself cannot be reassigned.

  • const numbers = [1, 2, 3] – Valid declaration.
  • numbers.push(4) – Allowed.
  • numbers = [5, 6] – Not allowed.

Example Code:

blocks.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<body>
  <script>
    const numbers = [1, 2, 3];
    numbers.push(4); // ✅ allowed
    document.write("Array: " + numbers);

    // numbers = [5, 6]; // ❌ TypeError
  </script>
</body>
</html>

JavaScript Operators

JavaScript operators are special symbols used to perform operations on operands (values and variables). They are the building blocks of most expressions and logic in JavaScript.

  • Operators are used for assignments, comparisons, arithmetic operations, logical evaluations, and more.
  • They help in manipulating data and making decisions in code execution.

Code Overview:

  • This code demonstrates common JavaScript operators such as arithmetic (+, -, *, /), comparison (>), and logical (&&).
  • Operators are used to evaluate and output the results directly on the web page.

Note: Always use parentheses to clarify complex expressions and maintain code readability.

Categories of JavaScript Operators

JavaScript offers several categories of operators used for various purposes:

1. Arithmetic Operators

  • Used to perform mathematical operations.
  • Examples: +, -, *, /, %, ++, --
  • let sum = 10 + 5;

2. Comparison Operators

  • Used to compare two values and return a boolean.
  • Examples: ==, ===, !=, !==, >, <, >=, <=
  • 10 > 5 // true

3. Logical Operators

  • Used to perform logical operations.
  • Examples: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
  • (a > 5 && b < 10) // true

4. Assignment Operators

  • Used to assign values to variables.
  • Examples: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=
  • x += 5 // same as x = x + 5

Best Practices for Using JavaScript Operators

  • Use === instead of == for strict equality to avoid type coercion bugs.
  • Use parentheses to make complex expressions clearer and easier to debug.
  • Combine logical operators wisely to build concise conditionals.
  • Be cautious with increment/decrement (++, --) inside expressions to avoid unexpected results.

HTML Text Formatting

HTML text formatting refers to the use of specific HTML tags to modify the appearance and structure of text on a webpage. It allows you to style text in different ways, such as making it bold, italic, underlined, highlighted, or struck-through.

Categories of HTML Text Formatting

HTML text formatting can be divided into two main categories: Logical Tags and Physical Tags.

1. Logical Tags

Logical tags convey the meaning or importance of the text without necessarily altering its visual appearance. These tags help browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies understand the purpose of the text.

  • <em> Emphasizes text, typically rendered in italics. It implies that the text carries special importance or requires emphasis.
  • <strong>Marks text as important, often displayed in bold. It implies the content is of strong importance.

2. Physical Tags

Physical tags directly affect how text looks on the webpage by changing the font, size, or style.

  • <b>: Displays text in bold without implying importance.
  • <i>: Italicizes text without any implied emphasis.

Here’s a list of commonly used HTML text formatting tags and their description:

HTML Formatting Elements

1. <i> – Italicizes text

Use the <i> tag to display text in italics without implying emphasis.

<i>This is italic text.</i>

2. <small> – Reduces the font size of the text

The <small> tag renders text in a smaller font than the surrounding text.

<small>This text is smaller than the rest.</small>

3. <ins> – Highlights inserted text

The <ins> tag marks text as newly added or inserted, often displayed with an underline.

<ins>This is inserted text.</ins>

4. <sub> – Displays subscript text

Use the <sub> tag for subscripted text, often used in chemical formulas or footnotes.

H<sub>2<sub>O

5. <mark> – Highlights text with a background color

The <mark> tag highlights text with a background color, similar to using a highlighter on paper.

<mark>This text is highlighted.</mark>

HTML Links, also known ashyperlinks, are defined by the <a> tag in HTML, which stands for "anchor." These links are essential for navigating between web pages and directing users to different sites, documents, or sections within the same page.

The basic attributes of the <a> tag include href, title, and target, among others.

Basic Syntax of an HTML Link:

Note: A hyperlink can be represented by an image or any other HTML element, not just text.

  • An unvisited link is underlined and blue.

HTML Links - Target Attribute

The target attribute in the <a> tag specifies where to open the linked document. It controls whether the link opens in the same window, a new window, or a specific frame.

Attribute Description
_blank Opens the linked document in a new window or tab.
_self Opens the linked document in the same frame or window as the link. (Default behavior)
_parent Opens the linked document in the parent frame.
_top Opens the linked document in the full body of the window.
framename Opens the linked document in a specified frame. The frame’s name is specified in the attribute.

HTML Lists

An HTML List allows you to organize data on web pages into an ordered or unordered format to make the information easier to read and visually appealing. HTML Lists are very helpful for creating structured, accessible content in web development.

Types of HTML Lists

There are three main types of lists in HTML:

  1. Unordered Lists (<ul>): These lists are used for items that do not need to be in any specific order. The list items are typically marked with bullets.
  2. Ordered Lists (<ol>): These lists are used when the order of the items is important. Each item in an ordered list is typically marked with numbers or letters.
  3. Description Lists (<dl>): These lists are used to contain terms and their corresponding descriptions.

    4. Basic Example of HTML Lists

HTML List Tags

Tag Description
<ul> Defines an unordered list.
<ol> Defines an ordered list.
<li> Defines a list item.
<dl> Defines a description list.
<dt> Defines a term in a description list.
<dd> Details the term in a description list.

1. Using HTML Unordered List or Bulleted List

Unordered lists are ideal for scenarios where the sequence of the items is not important.

The unordered list items are marked with bullets, also known as bulleted lists. An unordered list starts with the <ul> tag, and each list item begins with the <li> tag.

Syntax:

<ul>
<li>Item 1</li>
<li>Item 2</li>
<li>Item 3</li>
</ul>

Attribute: This tag contains two attributes which are listed below:

  • compact: It will render the list smaller.
  • type: It specifies which kind of marker is used in the list.

2. Using HTML Ordered List

Ordered lists are used when the items need to follow a specific sequence.

In an ordered list, all list items are marked with numbers by default. An ordered list starts with the <ol> tag, and each list item begins with the <li> tag.

Syntax:

<ol> <li>Item1</li> <li>Item2</li> <li>Item3</li> </ol>

Attributes:

  • compact: It defines the list should be compacted (compact attribute is not supported in HTML5. Use CSS instead.).
  • reversed: It defines that the order will be descending.
  • start: It defines from which number or alphabet the order will start.
  • type: It defines which type(1, A, a, I, and i) of the order you want in your list of numeric, alphabetic, or roman numbers.

3. Using HTML Description List

A description list is a list of terms, with a description of each term. Description lists are less common but very useful for definitions, glossaries, or any other key-value pairs of items.

The <dl> tag defines the description list, the <dt> tag defines the term name, and the <dd> tag describes each term.

Syntax:

<dl> <dt>Item 1</dt> <dd>Description of Item 1</dd> <dt>Item 2</dt> <dd>Description of Item 2</dd> </dl>

Here, <dt> (description term) is used for the term being defined, and <dd>(description details) is used for the description.

HTML Ordered Lists

HTML Iframes

An iframe, or Inline Frame, is an HTML element represented by the <iframe> tag. It functions as a 'window' on your webpage through which visitors can view and interact with another webpage from a different source.

Iframes are used for various purposes like:

  • Embedding Multimedia: Easily integrate videos, audio, or animations from platforms like YouTube, etc.
  • Including Maps: Embed maps from services like Google Maps directly into your site.
  • Loading Forms and Widgets: Incorporate forms or widgets from other sources without writing complex code.

Syntax:

<iframe src="URL" title="description"></iframe>

  • The src attribute specifies the URL of the document you want to embed.
  • Iframes can include videos, maps, or entire web pages from other sources.

Best Practices for Using Iframes

While iframes offer significant flexibility, they should be used wisely to ensure they enhance rather than detract from the user experience.

  • Security: Always use the sandbox attribute to restrict the iframe's capabilities unless you fully trust the content. This can prevent malicious scripts from running.
  • Performance: Iframes can slow down your page loading times. Only use them when necessary and ensure the embedded content is optimized for fast loading.
  • Accessibility: Provide alternative content for users who might not be able to interact with iframes. This can be done by placing text or links inside the <iframe> tags, which will only display if iframes are not supported.

HTML Forms

HTML forms, defined using the <form>Tags are essential for collecting user input on web pages. They incorporate a variety of interactive controls such as text fields, numeric inputs, email fields, password fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, and submit buttons. Over 85% of websites rely on forms to gather data from users, making them a fundamental component of modern web development.

Syntax

<form>
form elements..
</form>
